title: Staffing and Directing
summary: Staffing is employing and developing human resources for carrying out managerial and non-managerial activities; it involves determining manpower requirement, recruiting, selecting, training and developing people. It is a continuous process and part of human resource management (also remuneration, appraisal, promotion and transfers). Importance: right people for the right job at the right time; improves productivity; gives job satisfaction and keeps morale high; maintains harmony.

Steps in the staffing process: manpower planning (estimating the number and kind of staff needed), job analysis (systematically collecting information on a job; job description = statement of duties and responsibilities; job specification = qualifications, skills and abilities required), recruitment, selection, placement, induction, training and development, performance appraisal, compensation, promotion and transfer.

Recruitment is the process of finding and attracting suitable applicants for employment. Internal sources: transfers (shifting to another job without change in responsibilities and salary) and promotions (shifting to a higher job); advantages: managers know their people, and employees feel recognised; limitation: no fresh blood. External sources: media advertisements (newspapers, Employment News), employment exchanges, educational institutions (campus interviews), unsolicited applications, recruitment at the factory gate (casual workers), referrals (workers' unions, existing employees), private placement agencies. Recent trends: e-recruitment (naukri.com), outsourcing (RPO, a form of BPO), internships, walk-in interviews.

Selection is the process of choosing the most suitable person from among the interested candidates. Steps: screening of applications; selection tests (intelligence, aptitude, skill or trade, performance, personality tests); selection interview; checking of references; medical examination; job offer (appointment letter); probation period. Recruitment versus selection: recruitment attracts candidates (positive, simple); selection rejects the unsuitable (negative, complicated, many steps). Placement: determination and assignment of the job to the selected candidate (includes initial assignment, transfer and promotion). Induction: introducing new employees to the organisation and work environment.

Training increases knowledge and technical skills for a particular job (short term, job oriented, for technical and non-managerial staff); development refers to learning opportunities for growth in all areas and overall competence (long term, career oriented, for managers; teaches concepts and human skills). Benefits to organisation: less wastage, better performance, better use of men, machines and materials, positive attitude, reduced turnover, absenteeism and accidents and quicker adaptation to change; to employees: improved skills and career options, higher earnings, greater job capacity and satisfaction. Methods: on-the-job (job instruction or coaching, job rotation, assistant to a senior, understudy, temporary promotion) and off-the-job (lectures, conferences, case discussions, films, vestibule training – a workshop duplicating actual work conditions).

Performance appraisal means evaluating an employee's current or past performance against pre-determined standards (quantity, quality, minimisation of wastage). Compensation: base or primary (wages, salary, allowances) and supplementary or incentive compensation (monetary: bonus, commission, profit sharing; non-monetary). Promotion is advancement to a higher position with more responsibility, pay and status (basis seniority, merit or both); demotion is assignment to a lower job; transfer is a change to a job of the same rank and pay or to another unit.

Directing is instructing, guiding, supervising and inspiring people to achieve the organisation's objectives; it is the heart of management, 'management in action'. Importance: guides subordinates, motivates them, maintains discipline and rewards, supervision ensures work as per instructions, integrates activities and individual with organisational goals, leadership creates work environment and team spirit. Elements of directing: communication, supervision, motivation and leadership.

Communication is the process by which a sender transmits information to a receiver, a two-way process with feedback; it is the lifeblood of the organisation. Types: by channel – formal and informal; by direction – upward, downward, horizontal, diagonal; by mode – verbal (oral and written) and non-verbal (gestures). Barriers: semantic (symbols with different meanings, badly expressed message, faulty translation), psychological (lack of attention, loss by transmission and poor retention, premature evaluation, distrust), organisational (rules and regulations, status, policies, complex structure), personal (fear of challenge to authority, lack of confidence in subordinates, unwillingness to communicate, lack of incentive). Overcoming: consult others, communicate according to the receiver's needs, clarify the idea, be a good listener, give feedback and use informal channels.

Supervision: seeing that employees perform as instructed; supervisor clarifies orders, ensures facilities, guides, coordinates, detects errors; he is the link between management and workers, creates an ideal atmosphere, guides workers, ensures quality output and gives feedback. Motivation inspires a person to use his best capability: importance – maximum utilisation of resources, reduced turnover and absenteeism, sense of belonging, fewer complaints, attracts competent employees. Maslow's hierarchy of needs: physiological, safety and security, social, esteem (ego) and self-actualisation. Financial incentives: pay and allowances, bonus, commission, retirement benefits, perquisites; non-financial incentives: career advancement, status, employee recognition programmes, employee participation. Leadership is the ability to persuade and motivate others to work in the desired way; importance: influences behaviour, builds confidence and morale; qualities: competence, intelligence, honesty, integrity, initiative, perseverance and communication skills.

objective: Name the elements of directing (any two).

Fill in the blanks: (a) ______ is the process of telling people what to do and seeing that they do it in the best possible manner. (b) ______ refers to the process by which a person transmits information to another.
Give a specific term: (a) Barriers when sender and receiver interpret words and symbols differently. (b) The mode of communication that may be oral or written.
Fill in the blanks: (a) ______ results when receiver and sender do not trust each other. (b) The fear of losing authority over subordinates is called ______ barrier.
Give a specific term: (a) Privately operated organisations that introduce job seekers to employers. (b) Offices set up by the government to bring together job seekers and providers.
Name the process of finding and attracting suitable applicants; list two of its sources.
Recruitment; internal sources (transfer, promotion) and external sources (advertisements, employment exchanges).
State true or false: (i) Staffing is a one-time process. (ii) Training is job oriented.
Match: (a) Job description (b) Job specification with (i) statement of duties and responsibilities (ii) qualifications, skills and abilities required.
Name the need in Maslow's hierarchy: (a) respect and recognition (b) love, affection, friendship.
Give two examples each of financial and non-financial incentives.
Financial: bonus and commission; non-financial: status and recognition.
vsa: A company hires through references of existing employees. Identify the source of recruitment and mention its benefit.
Referrals; the people recommended are known to the company, so the recruitment is reliable, quick and cheap.

Name any one internal source of recruitment and give its limitation.
Promotion; limitation: the organisation does not get fresh blood or new ideas.
April 2026
Explain why a selection test is conducted by organisations during the selection process.
To measure the skills, abilities and aptitude of candidates against the job requirements and to eliminate the unsuitable.
April 2026
What is meant by 'Staffing'? / What is meant by 'Training'?
Staffing is employing and developing human resources for managerial and non-managerial jobs; training is increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for a particular job.

(a) Placement. (b) Induction.

Job description states duties and responsibilities; job specification states the qualifications and skills required.
Who is a leader? List two qualities of a good leader.
A person who influences others to follow his instructions; honesty, initiative and communication skill.
What is meant by manpower planning?
Estimating the quantity and quality of manpower required by the organisation to get the right number of qualified people at the right time.
sa: State any three points of importance of the 'staffing' function of management.
It gets the right people for the right job at the right time, improves productivity and gives job satisfaction and harmony.
October 2025
State two advantages and one drawback of internal sources of recruitment.
Advantages: managers know the abilities of their people and employees are happy with recognition of their performance; drawback: no fresh blood.
October 2025
State any three benefits of 'leadership'.
It influences behaviour towards organisational benefit, builds confidence and reduces wastage and builds morale and higher productivity.
October 2025
State any three points of importance of directing function of management.
It guides subordinates, motivates them and maintains discipline and integrates individual with organisational goals.
October 2025
Amit has to recruit 15 salesmen from outside the organisation. Explain any three sources he may use.
Media advertisements, employment exchanges and campus interviews (also referrals, placement agencies).
October 2024
Explain the first two steps of the selection process.
Screening of applications to check eligibility; selection tests to measure skills and abilities.
October 2024
Explain the difference between recruitment and selection (three points).
Recruitment attracts candidates and is positive and simple; selection rejects the unsuitable and is negative and complicated.
Explain any three benefits of training to the organisation.
Less wastage, better performance and reduced turnover, absenteeism and accidents.
Explain the functions of a supervisor (three).
Clarifies orders, guides and coordinates work and acts as a link between management and workers.
la: Explain the various types of financial incentives.
Pay and allowances (salary), bonus (cash or trips), commission on sales, retirement benefits (provident fund, pension, gratuity) and perquisites (rent-free accommodation, car allowance).
Explain the hierarchy of needs as given by Maslow.

Physiological needs (food, shelter), safety and security, social needs (love and friendship), esteem needs (respect and recognition) and self-actualisation; the next need arises once the lower one is satisfied.
Explain the first five steps involved in the process of selection.
Screening of applications, holding selection tests, conducting the interview, checking references and medical examination.
List any five specialised activities of a Human Resource Manager.
Manpower planning, recruitment, selection, training and development, performance appraisal, compensation and promotion and transfer (any five).
Describe the essential elements of directing.
Communication, supervision, motivation and leadership, each explained with its role.
What is meant by training? Explain the different methods of training.
Training increases knowledge and skill for a job; on-the-job methods (coaching, job rotation, understudy) and off-the-job methods (lectures, case discussions, vestibule training).
Explain the barriers to effective communication and how to overcome them.
Semantic, psychological, organisational and personal barriers; overcome by consulting others, adjusting to the receiver, clarity, listening and feedback.
